subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about the two parts that make every computer work: hardware and software. Hardware is the name for all the parts you can touch — the screen, the keyboard, the mouse. Software is the set of instructions, also called apps, that tell the hardware what to do. The big idea of the whole unit is simple: hardware and software must work together. One without the other does nothing. First, you learn what hardware and software are, and why a computer needs both. Second, you learn that hardware comes in three groups — input devices (that put information in), output devices (that show us the result), and storage devices (that keep our files). Third, you learn that input devices can be manual (a person works them, like a keyboard) or automatic (they work with little or no help, like a fire alarm sensor).
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say what hardware is (the physical parts you can touch) and give examples.
Say what software is (the instructions, or apps, that tell the hardware what to do) and give examples.
Explain why a computer needs both hardware and software to work.
Name the three categories of hardware — input, output and storage — and sort devices into them.
Describe some ways hardware and software are different (touch, damage, bugs).
Tell the difference between a manual and an automatic input device, and name examples of each.

concepts.title: What are hardware and software?
concepts.explanation: A computer is made of two things that work together. Hardware is all the parts you can touch. Software is the set of instructions — also called apps — that tell the hardware what to do. A computer needs both. Without software, the hardware does not know what to do; without hardware, the software has nowhere to run. Everything I can touch — the screen, the buttons, the glass — is the hardware. But on its own it is just plastic and glass.
concepts.example: The software is the instructions inside that tell it what to do. Another word for software is app.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell that the parts you touch are hardware, and the apps or instructions are software?

concepts.title: Three kinds of hardware: input, output, storage
concepts.explanation: Hardware comes in three groups. Input devices put information IN (a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone). Output devices show the result OUT to us (a screen, a speaker, a printer). Storage devices keep our files to use later (a USB drive, a hard drive). Your eyes and ears take things IN — they are like input. Your mouth talks OUT — that is like output. Your memory keeps things to use later — that is like storage.
concepts.example: A computer has all three too. Use your own body as the picture.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you place each device in the right group and say why? Watch the most common mix-up: a printer is an output device (it gives us a result on paper), not an input device.

concepts.title: How are hardware and software different?
concepts.explanation:
Hardware and software are different in important ways. You can touch hardware; you cannot touch software. Hardware can be dropped and broken; software cannot be dropped, but it can get a bug (a mistake in the instructions) or a virus. If a piece of hardware breaks, you replace the part. If software stops working, you install it again.

Tell two short stories and you can decide which is a hardware problem and which is a software problem.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: How are hardware and software different? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell a hardware problem (something broke — you replace it) from a software problem (a bug — you install it again)?

concepts.title: Manual and automatic input devices
concepts.explanation: There are two kinds of input devices. A manual input device needs a person to work it — you move the mouse with your hand, you press the keys with your fingers. An automatic input device works with little or no help from a person. Automatic devices are often more accurate, because a person can make mistakes when typing. Watch me type. I have to press every single key with my fingers. That is manual — it needs me. Now think about the fire alarm on the ceiling. Nobody presses it.
concepts.example: It senses smoke and goes off by itself. That is automatic.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell that manual needs a person and automatic does not? Watch the mix-up: a phone camera is manual (a person points it and presses the button), even though it feels clever and modern.

concepts.title: Look at a real device
concepts.explanation:
Every device is hardware and software working together. This is the one hands-on session, and it stays very gentle and safe.

First, let us find the hardware. Point to the screen, a button, the camera lens, the little speaker holes. Now let us find the software. These little pictures are apps, and each app is a piece of software. See?
concepts.example: This software is telling the hardware what to do. They are working together.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you point to at least three hardware parts and name at least two apps (software)?

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

I can say what software is (the instructions, or apps, that tell the hardware what to do) and give examples.
